records.name: Galicia
records.current_summary: Spain's Law 4/2023 for the real and effective equality of trans people (official gazette text) vests implementation of its administrative and education-facing provisions in the autonomous communities — this region's government among them. The parallel 2023 gender-recognition reform, letting registry entries change by self-declaration from age 12 without medical diagnosis, drew an international rights organisation to rank the country among autonomy-first jurisdictions.  The surviving record adds no Galician statute, ordinance, enforcement series or incident finding; regional value here is implementation posture under the 2023 framework, not separate restriction or separate protection.

sources.claim: Official gazette text (BOE-A-2023-5366) of State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will, depathologizes the procedure (no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement) and removes the former age-majority requirement for requesting it, with corresponding document adaptation; Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; the education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, this region's government among them.

Human Rights Watch, 16 February 2023, reporting the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law': legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The law strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict. HRW assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

sources.claim: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the national 'Trans Law' for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right to the registered change being grounded in the free development of personality (art. 10.1 CE). The law further defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances - the national framework the regional position in this record rests on.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) on the Spanish Congress's passage of the national Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment requirements; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. The law also strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. These are the national provisions this autonomous community implements under the same framework.

records.name: Chaco
records.current_summary: No Chaco-specific trans statute, quota-compliance finding or enforcement series survives in the record. The framework is national: a April 2025 national feature described the trans community facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' after decree roll-back of the Gender Identity Law, and a national hate-crime observatory reported 227 SOGI-motivated hate crimes for 2025 — up 62% year-on-year, its highest decade count, one every 38 hours, most attackers security-force personnel or unidentified — a baseline applying across the provinces including this one.  Visitor exposure in Chaco therefore tracks the national position: no provincial criminalisation survives in the record, amid a documented national surge in anti-trans violence and a contested federal law.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (10 April 2025) on the national framework binding every province: activists describe Argentina's trans community in a 'chaotic, desperate situation' under Milei; the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting the trans community are reported as worsened; this region carries no separate reporting, so the national picture stands as its baseline.

Agencia Presentes (19 March 2026) on the National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory's 2025 report: at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina in 2025 - up 62% year on year, the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, one crime every 38 hours - with trans women and travestis 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse; this province sits under that national pattern with no separate local record.

records.name: Mendoza
records.current_summary: No Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. That silence is not reassuring: interior provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real, and the country-wide security picture for trans and travesti people has sharply deteriorated.  What is documented is national. Per a March 2026 report by the LGBT news agency Agencia Presentes, drawing on the national hate-crime observatory's tally, at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were recorded in 2025 — up 62% year-on-year, the highest figure of the observatory's decade of operation, roughly one every 38 hours — with perpetrators predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, beatings the main modality, and the observatory attributing the surge to the national government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people. Attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of the president of an LGBTIQ+ organisation in a northern province. An April 2025 Blade feature described the transgender community as facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' amid government policies; the underlying page is no longer retrievable.

sources.claim: April 2025 Washington Blade dateline Buenos Aires: national framework binding this province - the Feb 5, 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments; the 1% Trans Labor Quota hires were dismissed and federal anti-discrimination agency INADI abolished in 2024; activists told the Blade police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under Milei, explicitly worse "even more so" in interior provinces without strong reporting infrastructure.

Agencia Presentes (19 Mar 2026) on the national hate-crime observatory record: 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina in 2025 - up 62% year on year, a ten-year record, one every 38 hours; perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, beatings the main modality, institutional violence up from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), 32% of 2025 incidents in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators strangers to their victims. This province sits under that national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

records.name: Ogun
records.current_summary: No regional protective statute, recorded incident series or documented enforcement divergence from the national framework has been documented for this state. The national framework applies in full: a 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and — as reported in August 2026 summarising a foreign government's travel advisory — also reaches assisting, attending or promoting same-sex ceremonies and LGBT+ organisations; religious criminal law in some northern states can carry the death penalty for same-sex conduct. The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.  The recorded violence pattern is national and recent: a 33-year-old transgender media personality and sex worker was beaten to death in the federal capital in August 2024, having reported a stabbing a year earlier and said she feared for her life; authorities ordered a discreet investigation. Mass arrests and detention of LGBT+ people remain common, concentrated in some northern states. The framework also bans public expression of identity and LGBT+ organising, and the advisory additionally flags short-notice curfews, network shutdowns and communal violence. The absence of state-specific records here reflects thin documentation rather than demonstrated safety.

sources.claim: BBC News, 9 Aug 2024: Nigerian police investigated the death of 33-year-old transgender TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', whose beaten body was found along a highway in the federal capital Abuja. She had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker, and had expressed fears for her life in the previous year. Useful to this record: nationally reported evidence (Aug 2024) that transgender people in Nigeria face lethal violence, with a police statement that 'preliminary investigations revealed that the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing' — documenting official framing as well as the killing; applies nationally, no state-specific divergence recorded.

Sahara Reporters, 19 Aug 2026: the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, a 14-year jail term under the 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and possible death-penalty risks in northern states under Sharia criminal law. Useful to this record: UK's official advisory states that LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, with 14-year imprisonment for same-sex unions and sharia death-penalty risk in some northern states — the national frame that applies in full in this southern state.

sources.claim: Sahara Reporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment federally; some northern states operate Sharia law where it can carry the death penalty; the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also criminalises participants and guests at same-sex weddings.

National-framework source applicable to Oyo: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). The twelve Shari'a-law states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — carry up to a death-penalty maximum for male same-sex conduct; Oyo is a southern state outside that regime, as the record states. The page documents that police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito') and that mass arrests recur across states (42 men arrested in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023), with no anti-discrimination protections. Supports the record's claims that the 2014 statute also reaches LGBTI organisations and that LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under the framework that applies in full to Oyo.

BBC Africa Eye's 15 May 2023 investigation by Ian Wafula and Tamasin Ford documents the 'kito' scheme the record warns about: criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular dating apps, entrap men, film them, and then extort, beat and even kidnap them, with the investigation interviewing 21 people about being 'kito'd'. Victims do not report to police for fear of being arrested or attacked, and the piece shows police-adjacent enforcement against the gangs, including a commander quoted as vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. National in scope (the underground scene described is Lagos-based), it substantiates the record's point that dating-app 'kito' extortion gangs are a nationwide risk for gay and transgender app users, a risk that applies in Oyo exactly as elsewhere in the country.
